data.text: Amara argued for taxing sugary drinks: price cuts consumption, reformulation, and funds prevention; costs of diabetes and heart disease fall on everyone.
Victor argued the tax is a regressive sin levy on the poor, that evidence of causation is association, and that reformulation undercuts the health claim.
Amara conceded the regressivity point but argued disease costs fall hardest on the poorest, so the levy is still justified.
Victor closed that the levy can lower purchases and raise revenue, but health outcomes are unproven; the tax is plausible, not just.
In the smartphone-ban debate, Victor argued a ban cannot define its target, is disproportionate since schools have narrower means, and teaches removal over governance.
Victor closed that the motion as drafted leaves enforcement, the override, and the definition of the banned object unresolved, and that this gap cuts against the ban.
In the compulsory-voting debate, Victor argued compulsion completes a duty owed, corrects the turnout gap favoring organized interests, and forces demand for easy, equal ballots.
Victor closed that Mei conceded turnout rises and only disputed magnitude; fines and donkey votes are design flaws fixed by civil penalties, a free vote, and no-fault abstention.
Victor defined the motion as a shorter standard week, same pay, phased in, not unpaid Fridays.
Victor cited the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931, which made the two-day weekend default with a ten-year transition and exemptions for continuous services.
Victor argued the Working Time Code Part IV already runs shift caps, rest periods and averaging, so a shorter standard week fits existing machinery.
Mei priced a fifth more staffed hours at roughly a tenth more on total recurring cost if labour is half of operating cost, in nine shift-based organisations.
Amara conceded the four-day rota was paid for with longer shifts and agreed sector trials should start with health and care.
